newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav airline sees 1.5 mln passengers in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav airline sees 1.5 mln passengers in 1997.

text.p: Yugoslavia's air carrier Jugoslovenski Aerotransport (JAT) on Thursday said it plans to raise its passenger volume to 1.5 million in 1997.
"By the end of the next two-year period,(end of 1999) we plan passenger volume of 2.5 million and cargo and mail traffic of 70,000 tonnes," JAT general manager Zika Petrovic told Reuters.
JAT expects to carry around 1.1 million passengers and 30,000 tonnes of cargo and mail in 1996.

"Although the number of passengers is still far below the five million per year we had before the disintegration of former Yugoslavia, what is positive is that 40-45 percent will be to international destinations," Petrovic said.

JAT's domestic market shrank with the former federation's breakup in 1991, while international flights were grounded in 1992 by U.N.-imposed sanctions on rump Yugoslavia -- Serbia and Montenegro -- for its involvement in the Bosnia war.
The United Nations last week voted to end the embargo.
JAT first returned to international markets in October 1994 with a promotion flight to Moscow after the embargo on travel, sports and culture was eased.
"In these two years JAT has returned to nearly all former European destinations and on some routes we practically have the same frequency as in the good old days," Petrovic said.
He said a Yugoslav delegation last week received assurances from U.S. authorities there were no obstacles to JAT's return to that market.

"We have already applied for permits and a decision should be made within the next ten or so days on intercontinental flights to the United States, and we hope Canada will follow suit," Petrovic said.
Another priority will be return to Middle East destinations such as Cairo, Abu Dhabi, Damascus and others, he said.
